ev.festival.text.1: There's a festival in town: processions, food, singing until dawn.
ev.festival.text.1.rome: Saturnalia! For a few days slaves and masters swap places, and everyone gives gifts and feasts.
ev.festival.text.1.athens: The Panathenaea: a procession carries a new robe for Athena's statue, and athletes and musicians compete in the games.
ev.festival.text.1.egypt: The festival of Isis: processions to the temple, music, boats on the Nile.
ev.festival.text.2: The harvest is in, and the whole district is celebrating: bonfires on the threshing floor, ring dances, tables set out under the open sky. The old folk swear they can't remember a year like it.
ev.festival.text.3: The great fair has come to town: rope-walkers, storytellers, sweet-sellers from every corner of the land. It's so loud you can't hear yourself think.
ev.festival.text.4: The new year is here: doors are hung with greenery, bonfires burn in the streets to drive out last year's troubles, and everyone wishes everyone luck.
ev.festival.text.5: A rich neighbour is holding a wedding and has invited the whole street: three days of music, food and dancing till you drop.
ev.festival.text.6: Spring has come, and the young people headed out past the edge of town at dawn: garlands, swings, songs, and by evening a feast right there in the meadow.
ev.festival.text.7: The Night of Lights: a lamp on every doorstep, little flames set floating on the water, and the streets packed until dawn.
ev.festival.text.8: News of victory has arrived. Everyone is out celebrating: warriors march past to the roar of the crowd, and food is handed out in the squares at the ruler's expense.
ev.festival.text.9: The craftsmen are honouring their patron: each guild carries its banner through the streets, the potters hand out jugs, the bakers flatbreads, and all of it to song.
ev.festival.text.10: A new ruler has taken the throne, and three days of celebration have been declared across the land. Heralds cry that this year's taxes will be merciful, and everyone wants to believe them.
ev.festival.text.11: Travelling players have arrived in the square: puppeteers, jugglers, a man who swallows fire. The whole district has dropped its work and come running to watch.
ev.festival.text.12: The longest day of the year. All night there are bonfires, people leaping over the flames and telling fortunes, and in the morning nobody can find their shoes.
ev.festival.text.13: A great holy day of your faith: prayers and a procession in the morning, then tables are carried out into the street and every passer-by is called in to eat.
ev.festival.text.14: The shortest days of the year. To call the sun back, fires burn everywhere, people give each other sweets and sit at table late into the night.
ev.festival.text.15: A festival of contests: wrestlers in the square, footraces around the walls, archers shooting at a straw target. The bets keep climbing, and the shouting carries far beyond the town.
ev.festival.text.16: The water festival: everyone drenches everyone, children shriek, the old folk pretend to be cross, and then they all dry off around the fires with food in hand.
ev.y_procession_run.text.1: A festival procession is passing through the whole city, and all the neighborhood kids are already there. And you've been told to stay home and sort beans.
ev.y_procession_run.text.1.rome: Today a triumphing general rides along the Sacred Way: a golden chariot, captives, wagons of plunder, soldiers singing cheeky songs. And you've been told to stay home and sort lentils.
ev.y_procession_run.text.1.athens: Today the statue of Dionysus is brought into the city in procession: pipes, masked revelers, bulls for sacrifice, and theatre afterwards. And you've been told to stay home and sort lentils.
ev.y_procession_run.text.1.egypt: Today the goddess's barque is carried to the temple: rattling sistrums, pipes, free bread and beer. And you've been told to stay home and sort lentils.
ev.y_procession_run.text.2: A bride from a noble house is being carried through the city: drums, a canopied litter, sweets flung into the crowd. And your mother has told you to stay home and pound grain in the mortar.
ev.y_procession_run.text.3: They say a rich man's menagerie is being led down the main street: spotted, striped, horned beasts in cages, and one with a neck as tall as the rooftops. And you've been told to stay home and scrub the pots.
ev.y_procession_run.text.4: The army is coming home victorious: horns, banners, captives, and the commander himself at the front. And you've been told to stay home and wind thread.
ev.y_procession_run.text.5: Masked dancers are coming down the street: fearsome masks, drums, stilts, and a dozen people under one cloth pretending to be a giant beast. And you've been told to stay home and spin.
ev.y_procession_run.text.6: The new governor is arriving in the city: guards, servants, a litter, heralds shouting his titles. And your mother has left you to guard the drying fruit from the birds.
ev.y_procession_run.text.7: A travelling troupe is parading down the street with music, calling everyone to a show by the gates, a tail of children trailing behind. And you've been told to stay home and sweep the yard.
ev.y_procession_run.text.8: The first sheaf of the new harvest is being carried through the village with songs, young men in garlands dancing in front. And you've been told to stay home and pick the pebbles out of the grain.
ev.y_procession_run.text.9: Tonight hundreds of lanterns will be carried through the streets – they say the whole city will glow like a river of stars. And your mother has told you to stay home and mend the basket.
ev.y_procession_run.text.10: An ancient holy relic is being carried through the city: people throw flowers under the bearers' feet, sing, weep for joy. And you've been told to stay home and fetch water.
ev.y_procession_run.text.11: An embassy from a distant land is passing through the city: outlandish clothes, gifts for the ruler, music nobody here has ever heard. And you've been told to stay home and twist rope.
ev.y_procession_run.text.12: A local lad has won at the great games, and now he's being carried shoulder-high through the whole city with songs. And you've been told to stay home and mind the hearth.
ev.y_procession_run.text.13: A great caravan is entering the city: dozens of porters and pack animals, bales of spices, drivers in bright clothes. And you've been told to stay home and weave a mat.
ev.y_procession_run.text.14: Today they're welcoming spring: girls in flowers, boys with green branches, songs filling the street, and a bonfire outside town at the end. And you've been told to stay home and clean the fish.
ev.y_procession_run.text.15: The ruler himself is passing through your city with his retinue: heralds, guards, servants tossing small coins into the crowd. And you've been told to stay home and knead the dough.
ev.y_procession_run.text.16: All the craft guilds are marching through the city with their banners: the cobblers carry a giant shoe, the bakers a loaf the size of a table. And your mother has told you to stay home and mind the neighbours' toddler.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.1: A thunderstorm raged all night. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} crawled under your blanket, and until morning you argued in whispers about who had made the sky so angry.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.1.polytheist: A thunderstorm raged all night. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} crawled under your blanket, and until morning you argued in whispers about who had made the Thunderer so angry.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.2: The wind tore at the roof all night. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} held your hand and told you a story made up on the spot – about a wind that got tired toward morning and went to sleep.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.3: The downpour broke through the roof right above your bed. You and {npc} spent until dawn putting pots under the drips and howling with laughter every time someone missed.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.4: Hail drummed on the roof like a herd running across it. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} counted the hailstones in a whisper, you counted the lightning, and somewhere in the third hundred you both fell asleep.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.5: In the night something howled outside the wall – maybe a dog, maybe not. {npc} silently climbed over into your bed, and being scared together turned out to be hardly scary at all.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.6: Thunder struck so close the walls shook. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} announced {g=npc_sex:he|she} wasn't the least bit afraid – and held on to the hem of your shirt until morning.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.7: The lamp went out in the middle of the storm. In the dark {npc} found your hand and whispered, "If anything happens, I'll protect you." {g=npc_sex:His|Her} voice shook more than yours.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.8: The storm moaned in the hearth as if alive. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} insisted it was a giant tossing in his sleep, and until morning you made up what he might be dreaming.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.9: In the night the ground shook – only a little, but the pots on the shelf rattled. {npc} clung to you, and afterwards you argued for ages about which of you had trembled more.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.10: It had rained for three days and the yard had become a lake. Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} launched bark boats from the doorstep, and you appointed yourself their king of the sea.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.11: Lightning split the old tree by the road. All night {npc} lay awake whispering about whether a spirit had lived in that tree – and where it would go now.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.12: The wind tore a shutter loose, and it banged until morning. You and {npc} took turns standing guard at the window with a stick – "in case it isn't the wind after all."
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.13: During the storm {npc} hid under the blanket head and all and called you in too: "The lightning can't find us here." And so you fell asleep – in the stuffy, warm, safe dark.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.14: The storm only passed at dawn. All that time your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} sang you a lullaby – off-key, losing the words, but louder than the thunder.
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.15: The wind howled through the cracks, and you had a frightening dream. You woke to find {npc} stroking your hair and whispering, "It's only the wind. Sleep."
ev.y_storm_sibling.text.16: As the thunder rolled, your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} shared a hidden sweet with you: "If it's the end of the world, we shouldn't meet it with empty mouths."
ev.mentor_offer.text.1: A craftsman down the street is looking for an apprentice. Lots of work, little pay, but he'll teach you everything he knows.
ev.mentor_offer.text.2: The potter at the edge of town has had his eye on you for a while: you've got the right hands, he says. Clay, kiln heat, clothes forever filthy – but a trade for life.
ev.mentor_offer.text.3: The master weaver in the next yard is looking for an apprentice at the loom. She's strict and quick with a slap, but her patterns are recognised in every market.
ev.mentor_offer.text.4: The carpenter who mended the neighbours' roof has asked you to be his apprentice. "Wood doesn't like to be rushed," he said. "In three years or so you'll understand why."
ev.mentor_offer.text.5: The tanner needs an apprentice. The vats stink enough to make your eyes water, but he eats better than half the street and knows every trader in the district.
ev.mentor_offer.text.6: The cloth dyer is looking for a helper. Your arms will be blue to the elbow, but he promises to share the secrets of colours he's never trusted to anyone.
ev.mentor_offer.text.7: The stonecutters' crew is taking apprentices. Their foreman, grey and half-deaf from the endless tapping, said: "The stone will teach you patience. I'll teach you the rest."
ev.mentor_offer.text.8: The cobbler with the shop by the gate is getting old and looking for someone to pass the trade to. Awl, waxed thread, a hundred foot-sizes in your head – and loyal customers.
ev.mentor_offer.text.9: The baker on the square wants an apprentice: up before dawn, kneading till your shoulders ache. But people come from distant quarters for his bread, and you'll never go hungry.
ev.mentor_offer.text.10: The old basket-maker weaves so fast your eye can't keep up. She offers to teach you – "while your fingers are young and still bend the right way."
ev.mentor_offer.text.11: The woodcarver who makes patterned doors for rich houses is looking for an apprentice. First years of sweeping shavings, and then, with luck, your very own first design.
ev.mentor_offer.text.12: The ropemaker in the long yard outside town needs an apprentice: walking back and forth twisting fibre, a thousand paces a day. It looks simple, but there's a lifetime of secrets in it.
ev.mentor_offer.text.13: The craftsman who grinds beads from coloured stone has noticed your nimble fingers. The pay is a pittance, but it's a fine craft and valued everywhere.
ev.mentor_offer.text.14: The tailor who clothes half the market is looking for an apprentice. Sitting hunched from dawn to dusk, pricking your fingers with the needle – and hearing every bit of gossip the customers bring in.
ev.mentor_offer.text.15: The master brickmaker is looking for a sharp apprentice: mixing, moulds, firing. "The town keeps building," he says, "so we'll never be short of bread."
ev.mentor_offer.text.16: The net-maker sits on his doorstep from morning till night, fingers flicking faster than sparrows. He offers to teach you: everyone who catches fish or birds needs nets.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.1: The guests dropped by "for an hour." They left after midnight, having eaten everything down to the spare flatbreads and praising your table loudly enough for the whole street to hear.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.2: An old friend dropped by with his companions "for just a minute." The minute stretched until dawn; by morning there wasn't a crumb left in the house, but everyone was friends for life.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.3: The neighbours came to congratulate you on your good luck and stayed till midnight. They celebrated it so thoroughly that all that's left of it is the dirty dishes.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.4: The guests came from far away, and custom says they can't leave hungry. You put out everything you had – and they honestly ate everything you had.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.5: You invited three, and seven came. Nobody knew two of them, but by the end of the evening they were the ones singing loudest.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.6: A noisy evening: the guests argued about prices, about rulers and about whose turn it was to host next. They decided: you again.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.7: A merchant you know brought his travelling companions round. They ate as if they hadn't eaten in a week and told stories of distant lands deep into the night.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.8: Old friends gathered at your place to remember their youth. They remembered everything – except that it was time to go home.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.9: The guests stayed late: first they ate, then they sang, then they ate again. In the morning you found someone else's sandals in the house and one guest still asleep.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.10: You threw a supper for the whole street. The food was gone in an hour, the talk went past midnight, and you made up with the grumpy old neighbour before the first course was over.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.11: The rain drove passers-by under your awning, and you, foolishly, offered them a bite. The rain stopped at midnight; your stores ran out much sooner.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.12: The guests came with a gift – a basket of fruit. They left without the basket, without the fruit and with half your pantry inside them, but happy. Which means you're happy too.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.13: You celebrated your birthday – though you've lost count of which one. There were many guests, even more good wishes, and the whole neighbourhood heard the singing.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.14: A guest from far away spent the whole evening teaching everyone at the table a song from his homeland. By morning the whole street knew it – and, unfortunately, was singing it.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.15: Some acquaintances stopped by "just to say hello." They said hello, ate, told you every bit of news from the past year and left as the sky above the roofs was turning pale.
ev.a_dinner_guests.text.16: The supper was a success: the meat was eaten, the flatbreads were eaten, even what you'd been saving for the holiday was eaten. The guests left happy, and you were left with empty pots and a full heart.
ev.t_road_robbers.text.1: On an empty stretch of road five men step out of the bushes with clubs and knives. One grabs you by the shoulder, another is already rummaging through your packs. Their leader, a scar running down his cheek, smiles almost kindly: “Your purse, and go in peace.”
ev.t_road_robbers.text.1.rome: On a deserted stretch of road between two roadside tombs, five men climb over a wall with clubs and knives – runaway slaves or ruined shepherds, there's no telling. Their leader, a scar running down his cheek, smiles almost kindly: “Your purse, and go in peace.”
ev.t_road_robbers.text.1.egypt: The caravan fell behind, and on the empty road between villages five men on donkeys surround you, armed with sticks and sickles. Their leader, a scar running down his cheek, smiles almost kindly: “Your purse, and go in peace.”
ev.t_road_robbers.text.2: On the mountain pass a felled tree blocks the trail. The moment you stop, six men rise from behind the rocks. Their leader, grey and unhurried, talks like a market trader: "This is a toll road. The price is your purse."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.3: At the ford, while you were taking off your shoes to wade across, four men with stakes stepped onto the bank. Their leader, barely more than a boy with a wispy beard, tries very hard to sound rough: "Purse over here, and then off you go across."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.4: In the forest the road narrows to a path, and suddenly branches snap ahead and behind. Five men, faces wrapped in rags. Their leader lazily toys with a knife: "No hurry, traveller. First we share."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.5: You had settled down for the night by the road when three "travellers" sat down at your fire. A moment later there were seven, and the most polite of them – clearly the leader – asked for your purse "for safekeeping."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.6: A cripple sat by the roadside asking for help to stand. You held out your hand – and the cripple got up on his own, while four more men climbed out of the ditch. "Thanks for your kindness," the leader grinned. "Now the purse."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.7: The old bridge over the gully has been blocked with a log. Five men with clubs stand on the far side, and their leader shouts: "Toll for crossing! The bridge is ours – we mended it ourselves. Almost."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.8: In a narrow ravine pebbles trickle down from above, and several men with slings and clubs jump down onto the path. The one-eyed leader spits: "Purse. Or we start counting your bones."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.9: On the road you're surrounded by ragged men with the bearing of former soldiers. Their leader, in a torn cloak that was once expensive, speaks wearily: "We haven't been paid in six months. Now you're paying."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.10: The fellow traveller you'd walked with all the way from the market suddenly whistled – and his friends stepped out of the undergrowth. "No hard feelings," he said, almost sincerely. "I even like you. Your purse, if you please."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.11: In the middle of a scorched plain, with nowhere to hide and nowhere to run, six men catch up with you. Their leader squints at the sun: "Hot today. Hand over the purse and let's part ways before we all boil."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.12: You sat down to rest by an abandoned shrine, and five men came out from behind the ruins. Their leader bows with mock reverence: "Make an offering, traveller. The spirits of this place are very fond of silver."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.13: There's no getting past anyone on a causeway through the marsh: three men with hooked poles ahead, two more behind. The pock-marked, cheerful leader spreads his hands: "You can see it yourself – there's only one road. Purse."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.14: The sun has set, and the nearest village is still far off. Shadows rise from the roadside bushes – four, five, six. The leader's voice comes out of the dark almost tenderly: "No noise now. Your purse, and go in peace."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.15: At the bend five men block the road, and their chief is a wiry old man with a staff. "I was robbing this road before you were born," he says. "Purse, and don't make me run."
ev.t_road_robbers.text.16: In a shady grove you stopped to drink at a spring – and someone was already waiting for you. Five men with clubs, and their leader chewing a blade of grass: "The water's free. Everything else isn't."
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} broke a clay lamp and blamed it all on you. But that evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} secretly brought you half {g=npc_sex:his|her} flatbread to make peace.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} ate the sweets set aside for the holiday and pointed at you. That night {g=npc_sex:he|she} whispered "sorry" and gave you {g=npc_sex:his|her} best toy.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.3: {npc} dropped the bucket down the well and said it was you. You got the scolding, but that evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} went fishing the bucket out {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} – "to make it fair."
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} tore the new mat and blamed it all on you. At bedtime {g=npc_sex:he|she} silently pushed {g=npc_sex:his|her} pillow up against yours – that's how the two of you say sorry.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.5: A smashed pot of oil, shouting, your name. And then {npc} secretly scrubbed the stain off the floor and confessed after all – though only once you'd already been punished.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.6: {npc} broke the spindle and hid the pieces under your bed. That, of course, is where they were found. In the evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} held out a clay whistle {g=npc_sex:he|she}'d made {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} – a peace offering.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} knocked over the dough tub and swore it was you. You got the telling-off, but all evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} followed you around making faces until you gave in and laughed.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.8: {npc} lost the knife nobody was allowed to touch and pinned it all on you. But in the morning you found a wreath of wildflowers by your bed – unsigned, but you knew.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} smashed the water jar right on the doorstep and said it was your fault. That night {g=npc_sex:he|she} hauled water for the whole house – enough for two.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.10: {npc} scribbled charcoal all over the freshly whitewashed wall and pointed at you. In the evening another drawing appeared on the same wall: the two of you, holding hands.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.11: The holiday flatbread went missing, and {npc} named you without a moment's hesitation. But at supper {g=npc_sex:he|she} slipped you {g=npc_sex:his|her} own portion and turned red to the ears.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.12: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} broke the weaving comb and blamed you for it. At bedtime {g=npc_sex:he|she} told you the scariest and funniest story {g=npc_sex:he|she} knew – which was almost an apology.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.13: {npc} singed the edge of the holiday blanket at the hearth and said without blinking, "It wasn't me." You got scolded. But that night {g=npc_sex:he|she} tucked that very blanket around you – burnt edge on {g=npc_sex:his|her} own side.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.14: {npc} untied the dog, and it ran off with the meat for dinner. You were declared the culprit. In the evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} brought you a bone – as a joke – and a handful of nuts – in earnest.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} trod on the neighbour potter's drying pots and promptly said it was you. You worked it off together afterwards: {npc} volunteered to knead clay for the neighbour right beside you.
ev.y_sibling_lamp.text.16: {npc} broke the old cup the household treasured and blamed it all on you. Under the blanket {g=npc_sex:he|she} whispered "sorry-sorry-sorry" for ages, until you forgave {g=npc_sex:him|her} just to get some sleep.
ev.c_help_work.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} helped you at work for the first time – very serious, tongue sticking out. Little was ruined, and there was enough pride to last the whole evening.
ev.c_help_work.text.2: {npc} carried your tools around after you all day and handed them over before you could even ask. Not always the right ones – but with such zeal that you didn't have the heart to scold.
ev.c_help_work.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came to work with you for the first time and asked questions the whole way. By evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} was explaining to the neighbourhood kids how it all works – almost correctly.
ev.c_help_work.text.4: {npc} took on the counting alongside you and caught your mistake twice. You pretended it had been a test.
ev.c_help_work.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} helped you from first light and by noon was so worn out that {g=npc_sex:he|she} fell asleep right in the middle of the job. You finished for both of you – smiling the whole time.
ev.c_help_work.text.6: Today {npc} worked beside you like a grown-up and even earned praise from a passer-by. That praise was retold about ten times over supper.
ev.c_help_work.text.7: {npc} decided to help and rearranged everything "the handier way." You spent half the day hunting for things, but it was impossible to be cross with such a proud little face.
ev.c_help_work.text.8: {npc} got {g=npc_sex:his|her} first real task from you – and carried it out so slowly and carefully you'd think the fate of the world depended on it.
ev.c_help_work.text.9: {npc} was at your beck and call all day: fetch this, hold that, run there. And in the evening announced proudly at supper: "We did good work today."
ev.c_help_work.text.10: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} truly helped you for the first time and ruined only one thing. It has been decided not to throw it away – as a keepsake.
ev.c_help_work.text.11: {npc} begged to be your helper and silently, snuffling, copied your every move. Suddenly you saw yourself from the outside – and started working more carefully.
ev.c_help_work.text.12: Under your eye {npc} made {g=npc_sex:his|her} very first piece of work alone. It came out crooked and funny, and you tucked it away in a chest like treasure.
ev.c_help_work.text.13: {npc} helped you until you got tired of explaining, and then started explaining to you how to do it better. Sometimes with good sense.
ev.c_help_work.text.14: Rain drove everyone indoors, and {npc} begged you to teach "at least something" of your work. By evening you'd realised that teaching is work too – and perhaps the most pleasant kind.
ev.c_help_work.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} volunteered to help and didn't complain once all day. The only complaint came in the evening – about a blister {g=npc_sex:he|she} is now very proud of.
ev.c_help_work.text.16: For the first time {npc} stood beside you from sunrise to sunset. People you know teased, "There's your replacement!" – and {npc} pretended not to hear, while simply glowing.
ev.school_offer.text.1: Your family wonders whether to send you to a schoolmaster. It costs money, and they need your help at home now.
ev.school_offer.text.2: At the edge of the square an old scribe teaches children their letters right under a tree – they trace the signs with sticks in the sand. He doesn't charge much, but he does charge, and there aren't enough hands at home as it is.
ev.school_offer.text.3: A neighbour, the widow of a learned man, has started teaching a few children from the street to read and write. She asks a fee – and wants you there in the mornings, when there's the most work at home.
ev.school_offer.text.4: A wandering teacher has come to the district for the winter, for food, a roof and a little pay. At home they argue: someone literate in the family would be useful, but who'll help around the house then?
ev.school_offer.text.5: A school of writing and reckoning has opened in town for the children of craftsmen and traders. At home they weigh it up: lessons aren't cheap, but nobody cheats a person who can write and count.
ev.school_offer.text.6: The schoolmaster on the next street is famous for his strictness: his pupils write neatly, and the cane is always within reach. At home they're deciding whether his lessons are worth the money – and the help you won't be giving at home.
ev.school_offer.text.7: A place has opened up with the schoolmaster – his last pupil moved away. It has to be decided quickly: the place is expensive, and you've got plenty of chores at home as it is.
ev.school_offer.text.8: The scribe who lives across the yard has offered to teach you to write in the evenings – for a small fee. At home they hesitate: there's never money to spare, and even less a pair of hands to spare.
ev.school_offer.text.9: You spend ages loitering under the school window, where children chant their letters in chorus. They've noticed at home – and now they're wondering whether to send you there, even though it isn't cheap.
ev.school_offer.text.10: A retired army clerk, lame and cheerful, is taking pupils. He doesn't charge much and tells stories of campaigns, but lessons will take every morning, and mornings are the busiest time at home.
ev.school_offer.text.11: The neighbours' children already go to the teacher and boast that they can write their names. At home they're working out what that kind of pride costs and whether you can afford it.
ev.school_offer.text.12: A guest at supper watched you counting on your fingers and said it would be a sin not to educate you. Now the family is arguing: a teacher costs money, and an extra pair of hands is needed now.
ev.school_offer.text.13: Now that the field work is over, the schoolmaster gathers children at his house. Payment is in money or firewood. At home they wonder whether they need that money and firewood more themselves.
ev.school_offer.text.14: You taught yourself a few letters by studying the writing on market stalls. They were surprised at home, and now they're thinking of sending you to a teacher – expensive as that is.
ev.school_offer.text.15: The teacher is willing to take you on, and you can pay in instalments. But instalments are still payment, and at home every penny and every pair of hands already counts.
ev.school_offer.text.16: The only good school is on the far side of town – half a day there and back. The family is arguing whether learning is worth that much money and your absence from home.
ev.c_first_love.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is in love: sighing, not eating, writing someone's name on every wall. You never knew your house had so many walls.
ev.c_first_love.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has suddenly started combing {g=npc_sex:his|her} hair three times a day and running to the well for no reason. There is a reason at the well, as it turns out – with bright eyes.
ev.c_first_love.text.3: {npc} is in love and now answers everything wrong. Today, asked "Have you eaten?", {g=npc_sex:he|she} replied: "Yes. {g=npc_sex:Her|His} voice is so lovely."
ev.c_first_love.text.4: {npc} sits on the doorstep all evening staring at a roof across the street. You asked what was so interesting about it. "Nothing," said {npc}, turning red to the ears.
ev.c_first_love.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is secretly composing songs. {g=npc_sex:He|She} can't sing and can't rhyme either, but the neighbours already know the name that gets rhymed with everything.
ev.c_first_love.text.6: {npc} gave someone {g=npc_sex:his|her} best belt and now goes about beltless but blissful. Won't say who – but the smile says it all.
ev.c_first_love.text.7: For the third time this week your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has volunteered to go to the market. Forgets the shopping but comes home glowing – and always by way of the same stall.
ev.c_first_love.text.8: {npc} has stopped eating and started sighing instead – loudly, with feeling, in front of everyone. You remembered yourself at that age and decided not to laugh. At least not in front of {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.c_first_love.text.9: At night you heard {npc} whispering someone's name over and over – practising saying it out loud. In the morning {g=npc_sex:he|she} acted as if nothing had happened.
ev.c_first_love.text.10: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is in love and now washes every day – unheard of. The house keeps running out of water, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} smells of herbs and hope.
ev.c_first_love.text.11: At supper {npc} asked how you knew you were in love. You started telling, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} had already stopped listening – gazing out the window with a silly smile.
ev.c_first_love.text.12: {npc} has been making something in secret for a week. It turns out to be a gift for someone {g=npc_sex:he|she} "actually hardly knows at all."
ev.c_first_love.text.13: {npc} came home with a black eye and a happy face. It turns out {g=npc_sex:he|she} was defending someone's honour – whose, {g=npc_sex:he|she} won't say under any torture.
ev.c_first_love.text.14: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} sits by the window all day long. The work isn't getting done, the jug isn't filled, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} knows by heart who walks down the street and when.
ev.c_first_love.text.15: The whole household knows who {npc} is in love with. The only one who doesn't is the person in question – and {npc} is sure nobody else has guessed either.
ev.c_first_love.text.16: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked your advice on how to win someone over. You gave the best advice you could muster – and {g=npc_sex:he|she} looked at you with pity.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.1: The harvest failed and grain prices have soared. Your granary is full, and one by one the neighbours come to ask – on credit, until better times.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.2: There was no rain all summer, and the fields burned to the roots. But your granary is full from last year, dealers are already offering triple the usual price, and the neighbours beg for even one sack – on credit.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.3: Locusts swept over the district in a cloud and left the earth bare. Your grain was in before they came – and now it's worth more than ever. Since dawn the neighbours have been waiting at your gate with empty sacks.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.4: Water lay on the fields until autumn, and the crop rotted where it stood. Your granary on the rise survived, and now everyone comes to you: some with money, some with pleading.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.5: Armies marched through the region and stripped it bare – everyone but you: your granary survived by some miracle. Prices in the market are insane, and there's a queue at your gate.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.6: In a single hour hail flattened everything growing in the valley. Your stores are full, and you know that many people won't have a handful left before the next harvest.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.7: The cold struck before the harvest could be gathered, and everything was lost. Prices rise every week, and people come asking you for grain to last till spring – on credit, on their word of honour.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.8: The crops blackened with some unknown blight, and the harvest failed across the whole district. Your granary of last year's stores has suddenly become the most valuable place for many days' travel around.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.9: A hungry year. First came the old widow from the next street, then the potter, then complete strangers. Everyone knows your granary is full, and everyone is asking – some on credit, some for mercy.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.10: The harvest has failed. A travelling dealer offers to buy all your grain at once – at triple the usual price. Over the fence, the neighbours are counting their last handfuls and waiting to see what you'll decide.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.11: It's midwinter, and everyone's stores have already run out – last harvest was meagre. Everyone's but yours. The neighbours come one by one, eyes lowered, asking for credit until better times.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.12: The roads are cut – war or bandits, nobody's sure – and grain has stopped coming into the district. Prices soared within a week, and your granary is full to the rafters.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.13: Rumours are creeping through the district that the harvest is bad everywhere and winter will bring famine. Prices are rising on rumour alone, and people are already knocking at your door – to buy, to borrow, to beg.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.14: The second failed harvest in a row. People are boiling grass and grinding bark, while your stores are full: you laid grain by when others laughed. They aren't laughing now.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.15: A hungry year. The headman came to you in person: everyone knows your granary is full, and he asks you to sell grain to the people – as much as you can bear to. Meanwhile the dealers are offering triple.
ev.v_greed_famine.text.16: Mice bred beyond counting this year and ate through the stores in nearly every granary. Yours, sealed with clay and shut tight, survived. Prices are climbing, and the neighbours are coming to you.
ev.marriage_later.text.1: Marriage comes up again. The years go by, and living alone is hard.
ev.marriage_later.text.2: The matchmaker is back – with a new name and the same old arguments: "A good person, hard-working, a solid household." The years go by, and each time it gets harder to say no.
ev.marriage_later.text.3: The {g:widow|widower} next door keeps dropping by "on business" and staying longer than needed. Yesterday {g:she|he} asked straight out: isn't it time the two of you stopped living alone, each in an empty house?
ev.marriage_later.text.4: Your friends are teasing you again over supper: they've all long since settled down, and you're the only one who hasn't. They laugh kindly, but afterwards, at home, it's especially quiet.
ev.marriage_later.text.5: At the festival you spent the whole evening beside a {g:merry widow|quiet widower}, and by morning the whole street knew. Now everyone is waiting to see if you'll make up your mind.
ev.marriage_later.text.6: Acquaintances in the next town have sent word: they know someone ready to marry – not young, but dependable. Going to meet them would mean making up your mind.
ev.marriage_later.text.7: One evening you caught yourself talking to the hearth. And the next morning the matchmaker was already on your doorstep – as if she'd sensed it.
ev.marriage_later.text.8: Someone you'd been friends with for years said one evening over supper: "What if we got married? We already know everything about each other."
ev.marriage_later.text.9: You were ill recently, and there was nobody to bring you water. As soon as you recovered you thought: perhaps it's time after all? Especially since the matchmaker has long been hinting at a good match.
ev.marriage_later.text.10: A respectable person from a good household proposes marriage – no passion, but respect and a sturdy household. "At our age," says the matchmaker, "nobody dreams of passion any more."
ev.marriage_later.text.11: The neighbours seem to be in league: wherever you go, the same person "happens" to turn up – unattached and perfectly pleasant. The hints are getting less and less subtle.
ev.marriage_later.text.12: For months now the spice seller at the market has been setting the best aside for you and refusing your change. Today {g:she|he} finally asked whether you'd like to come by for something other than shopping.
ev.marriage_later.text.13: The old folk shake their heads: it's not the custom to live without a partner at your age. They say there's a suitable person, and everyone is just waiting for your word.
ev.marriage_later.text.14: You dreamed of a noisy house full of voices. You woke in silence – and for the first time it felt not like peace but like emptiness. As if on purpose, the matchmaker dropped by that same day.
ev.marriage_later.text.15: Someone has taken to singing under your window – off-key, but very persistently. The singer was soon found: a {g:shy widow|middle-aged widower} from the next street, with the most serious intentions.
ev.marriage_later.text.16: People whisper that it's high time, or you'll end up alone for good. You pretend not to hear, but the proposal passed to you yesterday won't leave your head.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.1: A new levy on your trade has been announced: now every sale and every bale at the city gates owes a share to the treasury. Others in your trade grumble and whisper.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.1.rome: A new toll has been imposed: at the city gates and in the harbours a share is taken from every bale, and the tax farmers, the publicani, watch the goods more keenly than any guard.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.1.athens: The Assembly has voted a new market due: the right to trade in the agora now costs more and more often, and the collectors know every face.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.1.egypt: The farmers of the royal taxes have announced a new levy: in Ptolemaic Egypt every trade pays, from brewer to weaver, and the tax farmer's scribes are already going from shop to shop with their tablets.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.2: A new town wall is to be built, and everyone who trades or works will pay for it: a share of every good. The collectors are already listing shops, granaries and boats.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.3: The ruler has started a war, and the treasury needs money. A war levy has been declared: twice the old rate on your trade, and nobody knows for how long.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.4: The treasury has brought in new weights and measures – a little "lighter" than the old ones. You pay as before but get less, and the collectors make sure nobody measures the old way.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.5: The only bridge to the market now charges a toll on every load. Going round takes a day, and the collectors know that better than you do.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.6: The ruler is planning a lavish wedding, and everyone has been ordered to pay for it: a special levy on every trade and every field. Others in your line of work grumble – quietly.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.7: A new tax in kind has been announced: every tenth sack, bolt of cloth, basket – into the state storehouses. The collectors go round with their lists and measure by eye, always in their own favour.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.8: Now a market pitch costs not once a year but every market day. The old traders curse; the young ones work out how much they'll have left.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.9: The first thing the new governor did was raise every levy – "for the needs of the province." Judging by his new house, the province's needs are considerable.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.10: The high road is being repaired, and a new levy has been imposed on everyone who carries or sells goods. The road will be better – someday. The payment is due now.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.11: A new tax farmer has bought the right to collect the dues – a greedy man with a long memory. He has announced his own "fair" levy, and for a week now his men have been going yard to yard with sticks and lists.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.12: Now there's a charge for water from the common channel: for every field, every workshop, everyone who needs it for their work. Water used to belong to nobody – now it belongs to the state.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.13: A new levy has been declared – on every hearth and every workshop. The collectors peer into homes counting ovens, looms and working hands.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.14: A census has gone through the region, and everyone whose business is doing well has been put in a higher bracket – with a new, heavy levy. You're on that list.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.15: After a great fire in the capital, a rebuilding levy has been declared on everyone who trades or works. The collector is already at the door, and he has no sympathy to spare.
ev.j_any_new_tax.text.16: As if the old levy weren't enough, the local lord has added one of his own on the same goods. Now you pay twice, and each collector insists it's the other one that's illegal.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} hid your walking stick and spent half the day innocently helping you look for it. It turned up down the well. {npc} insists it fell in by itself.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} fed your dinner to the dog and insisted the dog had asked for it. The dog confirmed it – with its tail.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} dressed up in your holiday clothes and strutted about the yard pretending to be you. The likeness was uncanny – insultingly so.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.4: {npc} hid in a big basket and wouldn't answer for half a day while the whole household searched. {g=npc_sex:He|She} turned up on {g=npc_sex:his|her} own – once dinner started to smell good.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.5: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} decided to dye your hair with berry juice while you slept. For a week you went about with a purple streak, and {npc} called it "pretty."
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.6: {npc} taught the neighbourhood kids a teasing rhyme about you. It has to be said, the rhyme came out funny, and now you hum it yourself.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} decided to "help" and washed your sandals in the well. The sandals are clean. The well is not.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.8: {npc} put a burr on your bench and watched with innocent eyes as you sat down. The innocent eyes were betrayed by laughter – a moment later.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} pinched the sweets from your table and divided them fairly: the sweets for {g=npc_sex:himself|herself}, and for you a detailed account of how delicious they were.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.10: {npc} tied a little bell to your belt while you dozed. For half the day you couldn't work out why everyone in the yard turned to look as you passed.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} dug a "robber trap" in the yard. The first to fall into it was you.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.12: {npc} lugged a whole bucket of frogs into the house – "a present for you." The frogs scattered into every corner, and the entire household spent until evening catching them.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.13: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} announced that {g=npc_sex:he|she} was in charge now and ordered you about all day. You obeyed – and hadn't had so much fun in ages.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.14: {npc} told the neighbours in strict confidence that you have treasure buried under the floor. Now the neighbours look at you with suspicious respect.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} put a lizard in your bed – "so you won't be lonely." You yelled so loud the lizard certainly didn't feel lonely.
ev.c_grand_mischief.text.16: {npc} picked up a rude word from the grown-ups and came out with it in front of guests. You put on a stern face, but couldn't keep it up for long.
ev.c_h_diet.text.1: A physician you know watched you eat and delivered a whole lecture: less fatty meat and strong drink, more porridge, greens and walking. "Moderation in all things," he concluded.
ev.c_h_diet.text.2: At a feast your neighbour at table, an old physician, spent the evening counting how much you ate. At the end he sighed: "Another year of this and we'll meet at your house. On business."
ev.c_h_diet.text.3: You climbed a flight of stairs and couldn't catch your breath for a long while. A physician who saw it sat down at your table and started counting on his fingers: no fatty food, no strong drink, walk every day.
ev.c_h_diet.text.4: The physician held your wrist, was silent a while, then looked grimly over your dinner table. "The body is like a hearth," he said. "You heap it with logs and then wonder at the smoke."
ev.c_h_diet.text.5: You had to let your belt out another notch. A physician you know, dining with you, noticed and delivered a whole sermon: less meat and sweets, more greens and walking.
ev.c_h_diet.text.6: An old friend who became a physician told you bluntly over supper: "You eat as if famine is coming tomorrow. Famine won't come – gout will."
ev.c_h_diet.text.7: A physician treating your neighbour stayed for dinner and was horrified: "Meat in the morning, meat at noon, meat at night? Porridge, fish, greens, a walk – and, for heaven's sake, water instead of strong drink."
ev.c_h_diet.text.8: You complained to a physician that you sleep badly. He asked what you eat at night, heard your answer – and laughed for a good while before he began to explain.
ev.c_h_diet.text.9: A famous physician visiting the town dined with you and explained, free of charge – as he stressed – why you can't go on living like this: fat, sweets, strong drink and not one step on foot.
ev.c_h_diet.text.10: By evening your feet swell and your sandals pinch. The physician examined you, glanced at the table laden with food and said just one thing: "There's your illness – it's sitting right in front of you."
ev.c_h_diet.text.11: "At your age the body no longer forgives what it forgave in youth," said the physician, watching you reach for a third flatbread. Then came a list: what to eat, how far to walk and what to fear.
ev.c_h_diet.text.12: Your neighbour, a great lover of food, recently had a stroke. The physician, on his way out, looked in on you – and, seeing your supper, began the talk he'd come too late to have with your neighbour.
ev.c_h_diet.text.13: A physician turned out to be among your guests and spent the evening dissecting every dish in a whisper. At the end he said aloud, before everyone: "Our host should eat less and walk more."
ev.c_h_diet.text.14: The physician brought you a bitter brew for heartburn, and a lecture besides: herbs will help, but not instead of moderation – along with it. And walk. Every day.
ev.c_h_diet.text.15: Your stomach aches after every meal. The physician heard you out, looked at the laid table and said: "I can give you a remedy. Or I can give you advice – it's cheaper and works better."
ev.c_h_diet.text.16: A physician who knew you in your youth met you at the market and didn't recognise you at first. When he did, he shook his head, invited himself to dinner – and spent the whole meal explaining what needs to change.
ev.c_bully.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home with a split lip: the butcher's son, a head taller, has been taking {g=npc_sex:his|her} bread for days.
ev.c_bully.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home covered in mud: the potter's son, big and spoiling for a fight, has been shoving {g=npc_sex:him|her} into the ditch by the workshop for days.
ev.c_bully.parents.2: Have a word with the potter
ev.c_bully.parents.success.2: The potter listened, frowned and set his son to kneading clay from dawn to dusk. There's no time left for bullying.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.2: The potter waved it away: "Boys will be boys." And the jug you bought from him afterwards somehow leaked.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.2: A week later the potter's son took a tumble into that very ditch himself. Now he gives your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} a wide berth.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.2: {npc} hit back, but the potter's son was heavier. More mud, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.3: {npc} is crying in the corner: the headman's daughter mocks {g=npc_sex:him|her} in front of everyone and gets the other children to leave {g=npc_sex:him|her} out of their games.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.3: The headman turned out to be a fair man: his daughter apologised in front of everyone, and {npc} is being asked to play again.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.3: The headman took offence on his daughter's behalf and now looks at you as if you owed back taxes.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.3: {npc} answered the taunts so sharply that the whole street laughed – at the headman's daughter. She doesn't tease any more.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.3: {npc} tried to stand up to her, but the headman's daughter rallied every child on the street. More hurt, but {npc} doesn't hide any more.
ev.c_bully.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is afraid to fetch water: some older boys have taken over the well and demand a "water fee" – nuts one day, a flatbread the next.
ev.c_bully.parents.4: Go to the elders of the quarter
ev.c_bully.parents.success.4: The elders came down to the well and sent the "collectors" packing. Now {npc} fetches water with a proud air.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.4: The elders nodded and did nothing. The boys found out you'd complained, and the water fee went up.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.4: One day {npc} simply refused to hand over the flatbread and walloped the ringleader with the bucket. Nobody has charged for water since.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.4: {npc} hit back, but there were three of them. More bruises, but somehow the fear is gone.
ev.c_bully.avoid.ok.4: {npc} now goes to the far well. A longer road, and a longer grudge.
ev.c_bully.text.5: {npc} came home without {g=npc_sex:his|her} new cap: a rich merchant's son took it "to play with," while his servant stood by grinning. And not for the first time.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.5: The merchant was no fool: the cap came back, along with a handful of sweets "for the trouble."
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.5: The merchant didn't even come out – his servant said at the gate that the master was busy. The cap was gone for good.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.5: The next time, {npc} hung on to the cap so fiercely that the merchant's boy backed off. The servant, oddly, didn't step in – perhaps he'd been wanting to see that for a while.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.5: {npc} hit back, but then the servant stepped in. More bruises, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.6: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home in tears: the weaver's nephew, a head taller, stamped on {g=npc_sex:his|her} little clay animals and promised worse to come.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.6: The weaver gave her nephew such a dressing-down that the whole street heard. A day later he brought new clay animals himself – lopsided, but heartfelt.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.6: The weaver pursed her lips: her boy "wouldn't hurt a fly." Now she doesn't greet you.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.6: When the weaver's nephew came at {g=npc_sex:him|her} again, {npc} shoved him so hard he sat down in a puddle. Nobody touches the clay animals now.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.6: {npc} hit back, but the nephew hit back twice as hard. More tears, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.7: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} came home with scraped knees: the gatekeeper's son makes the younger kids bow down to the ground before him, and anyone who won't gets shoved into the dust.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.7: The gatekeeper took off his belt and explained to his son, in front of everyone, who was really in charge. Nobody is made to bow any more.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.7: The gatekeeper shrugged: the gate is his, and so are the rules. Now he lets you through last, too.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.7: {npc} didn't bow and didn't fall – it was the gatekeeper's son who ended up in the dust. They say there are new rules at the gate now.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.7: {npc} didn't bow and hit back, but the gatekeeper's son was stronger. Knees scraped again, but head held high.
ev.c_bully.text.8: {npc} won't leave the house: the tanner's son and his friends lie in wait around the corner and pelt {g=npc_sex:him|her} with rotten scraps.
ev.c_bully.parents.8: Have a word with the tanner
ev.c_bully.parents.success.8: The tanner listened, wiped his hands on his apron and promised his son would scrub the vats for a week. He kept his word – you could tell by the smell.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.8: The tanner laughed: "Scraps, so what!" Now laughter follows you whenever you pass his shop.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.8: The next time, {npc} didn't run but threw back – and hit the tanner's son square in the forehead. His friends scattered, laughing at him now.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.8: {npc} fought back, but there were too many of them. The clothes needed washing twice, but {npc} has stopped hiding.
ev.c_bully.text.9: The boys from the next street have been hunting your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}: they lurk by the corner and pelt {g=npc_sex:him|her} with pebbles. {npc} came home with a lump on {g=npc_sex:his|her} forehead.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.9: The grown-ups on that street turned out to be sensible people: the hunt was called off, and the ringleader wasn't let out of his yard for a week.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.9: The grown-ups on that street declared their children had nothing to do with it. Now the two streets are feuding, and there are more pebbles than ever.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.9: One day {npc} didn't run but marched straight at the bullies. They lost their nerve – and the hunt was over.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.9: {npc} tried to fight back, but there were too many. More lumps, but {npc} has stopped running.
ev.c_bully.text.10: The town guard's son takes every scrap of food from your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} and boasts that nothing will happen to him for it. {npc} has gone hungry for days.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.10: The guard turned purple: he won't let anyone shame his name, not even his son. {npc} eats {g=npc_sex:his|her} own lunch now.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.10: The guard rested his hand on his club and advised you not to slander honest folk. You didn't argue further.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.10: One day {npc} refused to give up lunch and struck first. The guard's son was stunned, and everyone saw that "nothing will happen" wasn't true.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.10: {npc} hit back, but the guard's son hit back twice as hard. Lunch was lost again, but there's less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} flatly refuses to go outside: the carpenter's son laughs at {g=npc_sex:his|her} patched clothes in front of everyone and shoves {g=npc_sex:him|her} if {npc} talks back.
ev.c_bully.parents.11: Have a word with the carpenter
ev.c_bully.parents.success.11: The carpenter turned out to have a conscience: his son came to apologise and even mended your gate – as a peace offering.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.11: The carpenter snorted: "Dress the child better and nobody'll laugh." You left seething.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.11: The next time, {npc} shoved back so hard that the carpenter's son sprawled in the wood shavings. Nobody dares laugh at the patches now.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.11: {npc} hit back, but the carpenter's son was tougher. More patches on the clothes, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.12: The baker's apprentice, a hulking lad of fifteen, waylays your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} on the road and takes every coin {npc} carries to buy bread.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.12: The baker listened, took his apprentice by the ear and sent him to knead dough all night. The coins reach the counter now.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.12: The baker brushed it off: he runs an oven, not a court. Now you always get the most burnt loaf.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.12: One day {npc} wouldn't give up the coin and raised a racket the whole street could hear. The baker's apprentice fled, and passers-by eyed him for a long time after.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.12: {npc} tried to fight back, but the lad was twice {g=npc_sex:his|her} size. One more bruise, but {npc} doesn't cry any more.
ev.c_bully.text.13: The healer's son, a know-it-all and a bully, calls your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} a dunce, and the other day he smashed {g=npc_sex:his|her} whistle on a stone.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.13: The healer apologised at length and made his son carve a new whistle. It came out crooked, but it whistles louder than the old one.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.13: The healer replied that his son is "simply cleverer" and advised you to take a calming brew. For a fee.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.13: When the know-it-all came at {g=npc_sex:him|her} again, {npc} shoved him so hard he sat down in the dirt and, for the first time in his life, had nothing to say.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.13: {npc} hit back, but the healer's son was quicker. More scrapes, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.14: The fisherman's son takes everything your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} catches by the water and laughs: "The water's mine!" Today {npc} came home empty-handed with a bloody nose.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.14: The fisherman, a straightforward man, cuffed his son on the spot. The next day the boy brought you fresh fish – "as payment."
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.14: The fisherman said the water really is theirs, and children can sort it out among themselves. You don't buy his fish any more.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.14: {npc} kept the catch and pushed the bully into the water. He climbed out wet and quiet – and doesn't pick fights any more.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.14: {npc} hit back, and they both ended up in the water. The bully climbed out first and laughed louder, but {npc} isn't afraid any more.
ev.c_bully.text.15: A great hulking herd boy chases your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} off with a stick whenever {npc} goes near the pasture, and has already torn {g=npc_sex:his|her} shirt.
ev.c_bully.parents.15: Go to the owner of the herd
ev.c_bully.parents.success.15: The herd's owner threatened to turn the boy off without pay. He keeps his stick to himself now.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.15: The herd's owner said he needs a herd boy more than he needs your friendship. The shirt had to be mended again.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.15: {npc} cut a stick just as good, and the herd boy, seeing it, preferred to come to terms. Now they're practically friends.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.15: {npc} stood up to the herd boy, but his stick was longer. More bruises, but less fear.
ev.c_bully.text.16: The moneylender's son shoves your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} into the mud in front of everyone, sneering that half the street is in debt to his family. {npc} came home filthy and silent.
ev.c_bully.parents.success.16: The moneylender, surprisingly, was embarrassed: a bad name is bad for business. His son got a thrashing, and you get a polite bow whenever you meet.
ev.c_bully.parents.failure.16: The moneylender listened, smiled and asked whether you might need a loan. And that was the end of the conversation.
ev.c_bully.fight.success.16: {npc} answered the next shove with such a thump that the moneylender's son sat down in the mud himself. Now he's the first to say hello.
ev.c_bully.fight.failure.16: {npc} hit back, but the moneylender's son brought reinforcements. More bruises, but less fear.
ev.a_promotion.text.1: Your superior promises you the senior post if you name whoever has been stealing supplies from the storeroom. You know who: your workmate, who has a sick wife and three children.
ev.a_promotion.text.2: Lamp oil keeps vanishing from the storeroom, and your superior promises the senior post to whoever names the thief. You know who it is: the old man who has worked beside you for thirty years and will retire next year.
ev.a_promotion.text.3: At night you saw your workmate carrying a little sack of grain out under his cloak. In the morning your superior announced: whoever names the thief becomes senior. Your workmate caught your eye and went pale.
ev.a_promotion.text.4: Your superior took you aside: "I need a senior I can trust. Prove it – tell me who's stealing." You know: the new lad, the one feeding a hungry family.
ev.a_promotion.title.5: The One Who Covered for You
ev.a_promotion.text.5: Little by little things go missing from the common stores – oil, bread, cloth. Your superior promises the senior post to whoever helps find the thief. You know who it is: the workmate who once covered for you.
ev.a_promotion.text.6: Your workmate is stealing to pay off his debts – you know it for certain, he let it slip himself. And your superior has just promised the senior post to whoever names the thief.
ev.a_promotion.text.7: The workmate who has always needled you is pilfering supplies from the store – you saw it yourself. Your superior offers the senior post for the thief's name. Revenge and promotion – in a single word.
ev.a_promotion.text.8: The stores don't tally, and your superior is hunting for whoever is taking them. You know it's your workmate: he carries part of the supplies to a sick old neighbour. The senior post – for one name.
ev.a_promotion.text.9: Your superior gathered everyone and demanded the thief's name, promising the senior post. Everyone is silent, staring at the floor. You know who it is – and you know he's staring at the floor harder than anyone.
ev.a_promotion.text.10: It's been a hungry year, and food keeps vanishing from the storeroom. You know who's taking it: a workmate with five hungry mouths at home. Your superior offers the senior post for his name.
ev.a_promotion.text.11: The new helper, just a boy, has been taking things from the storeroom bit by bit – you caught him at it, and he begged you in tears to keep quiet. Your superior promises the senior post to whoever names the thief.
ev.a_promotion.text.12: The thief is your childhood friend – the two of you started this job together. Your superior doesn't know that, but he promises the senior post to whoever points out the culprit.
ev.a_promotion.text.13: Your superior suspects everyone of the theft, you included. His offer: name the thief and you get the senior post and a clean name. You know who it is: a workmate with crippled hands who'll never be taken on anywhere else.
ev.a_promotion.text.14: The senior is retiring, and the post could be yours – if you help find whoever is pilfering tools and supplies. You know: it's your workmate, who sells them to pay the healer for his sick child.
ev.a_promotion.text.15: You found a sack of stolen goods hidden in a corner of the store – and recognised the knot on it, one only your workmate ties. Your superior promises the senior post to whoever names the thief.
ev.a_promotion.text.16: Your workmate once nursed you through an illness, and now he's stealing from the storeroom – you saw it with your own eyes. Your superior promises the senior post for the thief's name, and he's looking straight at you.
ev.c_new_faith.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has taken up a new teaching: goes to gatherings at night, talks of saving the soul and pities everyone who still clings to {faith}.
ev.c_new_faith.text.1.rome: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} now worships some eastern goddess: wears white linen, fasts before the rites and says the Roman gods are for people who've never seen true mysteries.
ev.c_new_faith.text.1.athens: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} trails after a wandering philosopher: barefoot, in an old cloak, arguing with everyone in the agora and insisting that wealth is a burden and family custom an empty habit.
ev.c_new_faith.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} keeps going off to the hills to a hermit whose disciples gather around him at night. Back home, {g=npc_sex:he|she} says that {faith} as your household keeps it is nothing but heartless ritual.
ev.c_new_faith.text.3: A wandering preacher has come to town, and {npc} never misses one of his night-time talks. At home {g=npc_sex:he|she} is giving away {g=npc_sex:his|her} belongings and calling it "liberation."
ev.c_new_faith.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} secretly goes to night gatherings where the faith is read in a way the temple does not teach. {g=npc_sex:He|She} says {g=npc_sex:he|she} has found a truth there that home never offered.
ev.c_new_faith.text.5: {npc} has joined a community that fasts for three days at a time and keeps silent vigils at night. {g=npc_sex:He|She} has grown thin, glows from within and hardly speaks to you.
ev.c_new_faith.text.6: A visiting foreigner teaches that all are equal before heaven – master and servant alike. {npc} attends his night-time talks and has already quarrelled with half the neighbours over it.
ev.c_new_faith.text.7: A woman has appeared in the district who, they say, can see the future. At night people gather around her, and {npc} is in the front row. The old rites, {g=npc_sex:he|she} says, are no longer needed.
ev.c_new_faith.text.8: {npc} has fallen in with people who expect the world to end by next spring. They meet at night, pray until dawn and urge everyone to sell their property before it's too late.
ev.c_new_faith.text.9: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has found a teacher – a sage who says wealth and ritual are empty and only the heart matters. They argue about the soul all night, and by day {npc} looks at your house as if it were a cage.
ev.c_new_faith.text.10: {npc} goes to secret gatherings where people sing and dance to exhaustion to "see the light." {g=npc_sex:He|She} comes home at dawn – happy and a stranger. And {faith}, {g=npc_sex:he|she} says, is for people who are afraid to dance.
ev.c_new_faith.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has announced that {g=npc_sex:he|she} has taken up a new teaching and a new name. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asks you never again to use the old one you gave, and goes off at night to {g=npc_sex:his|her} new fellow believers.
ev.c_new_faith.text.12: {npc} now dresses only in white, eats no meat and goes at night to people who call each other "the pure." {g=npc_sex:He|She} answers your questions gently and condescendingly, as if to a child.
ev.c_new_faith.text.13: A wandering healer cured a neighbour's limp, and since then crowds gather around him at night. {npc} goes to him every night and says the true power lies with him, not where you've prayed all your life.
ev.c_new_faith.text.14: At supper {npc} said openly for the first time that {faith} no longer means anything to {g=npc_sex:him|her}: {g=npc_sex:he|she} now has new teachers and night gatherings that can't be spoken of.
ev.c_new_faith.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} wants to join a community of the new teaching: everything is shared there, they work by day and pray by night. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asks for your blessing – or at least that you not stand in the way.
ev.c_new_faith.text.16: The neighbours whisper that {npc} goes at night to where the followers of the new teaching gather, and even brings others along. You asked straight out – and {npc} didn't deny it: "Yes. And you should come too."
ev.y_cheat_school.text.1: Tomorrow the teacher will make you recite a long passage by heart, and you haven't learned half of it. Your benchmate offers to prompt you for a handful of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.1.rome: Tomorrow the teacher will make you recite the Twelve Tables by heart, and you haven't learned half of them. Your benchmate offers to prompt you for a handful of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.1.athens: Tomorrow the teacher will make you recite a book of the Iliad by heart, and you haven't learned half of it. Your benchmate offers to prompt you for a handful of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.1.egypt: Tomorrow the teacher will give a dictation of Greek maxims, and you haven't learned half of them. Your benchmate offers to prompt you for a handful of dates.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.2: Tomorrow the teacher will test sums in your head – fast, in turn, no mistakes allowed. You get muddled past twenty, and your benchmate offers to whisper the answers in exchange for your lunch.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.3: Tomorrow you have to write from memory every sign learned this month, and you remember half at most. Your benchmate offers to whisper them to you – for your new writing stick.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.4: The teacher told everyone to learn twenty wise sayings and will test each pupil tomorrow. You've learned six. Your benchmate knows them all – and is willing to whisper for a handful of dried berries.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.5: Tomorrow it's the long song of the ancient heroes, by heart, in front of everyone. You're stuck halfway through, and the boy on the bench behind offers to prompt you for a couple of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.6: The teacher will ask for the names of all the rulers in order – from the most ancient on. You mix up even the last three. Your benchmate, who has a memory like an old scribe's, will whisper them for your flatbread.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.7: Tomorrow you must recite the old laws word for word. You've learned the beginning and the end, but the middle is a fog. Your benchmate promises to prompt you for a spoonful of honey.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.8: The teacher is giving a dictation, and every mistake earns a stroke. You're unsure of half the words. Your benchmate offers to sit closer and whisper – for your supper.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.9: Tomorrow there's a test on weights and measures: how much of what fits into what. You're hopelessly confused by it all. A crafty benchmate offers to whisper the answers and show them on his fingers for a handful of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.10: Tomorrow an important visitor comes to the school, and the teacher wants to show off his best pupils – you'll be called on to recite too. You're not ready. Your benchmate winks: "I'll prompt you. For your whistle."
ev.y_cheat_school.text.11: The teacher will ask the names of the stars – which rise when. You spent all week looking at the sky, but apparently in the wrong place. Your benchmate is ready to whisper for a handful of dried fruit.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.12: Tomorrow the teacher will test words of a foreign tongue – the traders' language, useful and hard. You remember a third at best. Your benchmate, who grew up by the market, speaks it fluently and will whisper for a couple of nuts.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.13: Tomorrow everyone must retell an ancient legend word for word. You remember how it ended, but not how it got there. Your benchmate offers to prompt you for your share of lunch.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.14: Yesterday you stumbled in class, and the teacher promised to test you again – tomorrow. You still haven't managed to learn it. Your benchmate, seeing your face, whispers: "Sit next to me, I'll help. Nuts later."
ev.y_cheat_school.text.15: You have to learn by heart the list of every river and mountain in the land – as long as the road itself. You remember only the beginning. Your benchmate offers prompts in exchange for your lunches for the next two days.
ev.y_cheat_school.text.16: Tomorrow the teacher will have you recite the long precepts of the ancient sages. You've read them so many times the words have turned to mush. Your benchmate, top of the class and a sly one, promises to whisper for a handful of nuts.
